title: Complexity of Non-Log-Concave Sampling in Fisher Information

paper.title: Complexity of Non-Log-Concave Sampling in Fisher Information
paper.abstract:
Abstract We study the query complexity of obtaining a relative Fisher information guarantee for sampling from a log-smooth non-log-concave distribution; this is a sampling analog of finding an approximate stationary point in optimization.
Our algorithm is based on the proximal sampler, which is an implicit discretization of the Langevin diffusion, and requires an implementation of the backward step known as the restricted Gaussian oracle (RGO).
We show that by leveraging the recent results for log-concave sampling with high-accuracy guarantees in Rényi divergence, we can obtain an approximate RGO implementation that—when used with the proximal sampler—yields a complexity guarantee in relative Fisher information that inherits the same dimension dependence as log-concave sampling, and improves upon prior work for non-log-concave sampling.
We also show a converse reduction that any improvement in the dimension dependence in relative Fisher information for non-log-concave sampling will yield an improved dimension dependence for high-accuracy log-concave sampling.

sections.heading: 1.1 Motivation and background
sections.text:
What is the complexity of sampling from a smooth distribution π ∝ exp ⁡ ( − f ) \pi\propto\exp(-f) over ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} ? When π \pi is log-concave or satisfies an isoperimetric inequality, then this question is well-studied, with many results providing iteration complexity guarantees which scale polynomially in the dimension and the isoperimetric constants; see [ 13 ] for an introduction to some of these developments. In this work, we are interested in the opposite scenario, in which π \pi is allowed to be highly non-log-concave, with the only assumption being that f f is L L -smooth, in the sense that − L ​ I ⪯ ∇ 2 f ⪯ L ​ I -LI\preceq

In this case, simple worst-case examples demonstrate that generating a sample close in total variation distance to π \pi can require exponentially many queries to f f (e.g., with respect to the ambient dimension d d ; see [ 18 ] .). One way to overcome this difficulty is to impose additional problem structure, such as assuming that π \pi is a mixture of strongly log-concave distributions [ 21 ] or to assume that an annealing path has small “action” [ 15 ] , which requires designing tailor-made algorithms for each problem class under consideration. Another approach is to weaken the notion of progress by seeking an approximately “stationary” solution. The latter idea has been especially fruitful in the sister field of optimization [ 24 ] , namely to minimize (or find a stationary point of) an objective function f : ℝ d → ℝ f\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}	o\mathbb{R} , in which the corresponding question becomes: How many queries to ∇ f

In the case where f f is L L -smooth but potentially non-convex, gradient descent finds such an approximate stationary point in O ⁡ ( 1 / ε 2 ) O(1/\varepsilon^{2}) iterations, and this rate is optimal in high dimension [ 5 ] . The optimal complexity in low dimension is still open, and it turns out that the results of this paper take on an interesting interpretation in light of this story; see Section 1.3 below. Although finding a stationary point is still a far cry from finding a global optimum, it is often the starting point for deeper investigations, such as the development of algorithms which escape “undesirable” stationary points (e.g., strict saddles). More broadly, this theory has the advantage of having great generality, as it is one of the few frameworks available to quantitatively study general non-convex optimization problems. Developing an analogous theory for the task of sampling is more subtle, as one must first decide on a suitable definition of an “approximate stationary point”. Such a definition was proposed in [ 3 ] , and it is based on the celebrated JKO theorem [ 20 ] which interprets the Langevin diffusion as a gradient flow, as explained next. Approximate stationarity in sampling admits a compelling interpretation as measuring closeness to metastability . Indeed, it is well-established that in the presence of free energy barriers, e.g., produced by well-separated modes of the target distribution π \pi , local Markov chains often get stuck at certain distributions which persist for exponential stretches of time, called metastable states. Although the concept of a metastable state is only loosely defined, in light of ( 2 ), we can view the relative Fisher information as a quantitative measure of metastability, since it implies that a measure ρ ho with small relative Fisher information will experience slow decrease of the KL divergence under the Langevin diffusion. For example, when π \pi is a mixture of Gaussians, [ 8 ] showed that a FI guarantee 𝖥𝖨 ( ρ ∥ π ) ≤ ε 2 \mathsf{FI}(ho\,\|\,\pi)\leq\varepsilon^{2} implies mixing for each of the components which have non-trivial mass under ρ ho . More recently, [ 25 ] showed that if each π k \pi_{k} satisfies a functional inequality (e.g., log-Sobolev), then 𝖥𝖨 ( ρ ∥ π ) ≤ ε 2 \mathsf{FI}(ho\,\|\,\pi)\leq\varepsilon^{2} implies that ρ ho is close in KL divergence to a reweighted mixture ∑ k = 1 K w k ′ ​ π k \sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}^{\prime}\pi_{k} for some (explicit) weights w 1 ′ , … , w K ′ w_{1}^{\prime},\dots,w_{K}^{\prime} . Generally, these results indicate that the complexity of stationarity in sampling captures the complexity of local mixing, which is a useful complement to worst-case global mixing results for non-log-concave sampling. There remains, however, a gap between the upper and lower bounds in the sequential setting, leading to the question of determining an optimal algorithm for local mixing. In particular, analogously to the picture for optimization, is an optimal algorithm given by some discretization of the Langevin diffusion—the sampling equivalent of the gradient flow—and if so, which one? In this work, we close this gap and answer this question affirmatively. We develop an algorithm, based on the proximal sampler [ 22 , 7 ] , which achieves the optimal complexity of O ⁡ ( 1 / ε 2 ) O(1/\varepsilon^{2}) up to logarithmic factors. Moreover, as we discuss below, the dimension dependence of our result is the best possible without further advances in the complexity of log-concave sampling.

sections.heading: 1.2 Contributions
sections.text: Our results are based on the proximal sampler algorithm, which is reviewed in Section 2 . Briefly, the proximal sampler first augments the target distribution π X ​ ( x ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( − f ⁡ ( x ) ) \pi^{X}(x)\propto\exp(-f(x)) into a joint density over two variables, π X ​ Y ​ ( x , y ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( − f ⁡ ( x ) − 1 2 ​ h ​ ‖ y − x ‖ 2 ) \pi^{XY}(x,y)\propto\exp(-f(x)-\frac{1}{2h}\,\|y-x\|^{2}) , and then applies Gibbs sampling. Concretely, this consists of alternating between the following two steps: given X X , sample Y ∼ π Y | X = 𝒩 ⁡ ( X , h ​ I d ) Y\sim\pi^{Y\mid X}=\mathcal{N}(X,hI_{d}) ; given Y Y , sample X ∼ π X | Y X\sim\pi^{X\mid Y} , where π X | Y \pi^{X\mid Y} is known as the restricted Gaussian oracle (RGO). When π X \pi^{X} is log-smooth and satisfies an isoperimetric inequality, such as a log-Sobolev inequality, [ 7 ] shows a high-accuracy guarantee for the proximal sampler in Rényi divergence. When π X \pi^{X} is log-smooth and strongly log-concave, [ 31 ] shows a high-accuracy guarantee for the proximal sampler in relative Fisher information. In this paper, we work only under the assumption that π X \pi^{X} is log-smooth, without assuming log-concavity or isoperimetry. Our first contribution is to show that under log-smoothness alone, the relative Fisher information decays in an average sense along the proximal sampler. Namely, we establish that 𝖥𝖨 ( ρ ¯ K X ∥ π X ) ≤ 1 K ∑ k = 1 K 𝖥𝖨 ( ρ k X ∥ π X ) ≤ 𝖪𝖫 0 h ⁡ ( 1 − L ​ h 2 ) ​ K , \displaystyle\mathsf{FI}(\bar{\rho}_{K}^{X}\,\|\,\pi^{X})\leq\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathsf{FI}(\rho_{k}^{X}\,\|\,\pi^{X})\leq\frac{\mathsf{KL}_{0}}{h\,(1-\frac{Lh}{2})\,K}\,, (3) where ρ k X \rho_{k}^{X} denotes the law of the k k -th iterate of the proximal sampler algorithm, ρ ¯ K X ≔ 1 K ​ ∑ k = 1 K ρ k X \bar{\rho}_{K}^{X}\coloneqq\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\rho_{k}^{X} is the averaged measure, and 𝖪𝖫 0 ≔ 𝖪𝖫 ( ρ 0 X ∥ π X ) \mathsf{KL}_{0}\coloneqq\mathsf{KL}(\rho_{0}^{X}\,\|\,\pi^{X}) ; see Theorem 1 below. Establishing the corresponding guarantee ( 3 ) for the proximal sampler is more involved since it requires tracking the relative Fisher information along simultaneous evolution of both arguments along the heat flow and its time reversal, and here we leverage the recent results of [ 31 ] . However, ( 3 ) is not yet an algorithmic result, as it assumes that we can implement the RGO exactly. Our next contributions address this point. We note this already improves upon the O ⁡ ( L 2 ​ d ​ 𝖪𝖫 0 ε 4 ) O(\frac{L^{2}d\,\mathsf{KL}_{0}}{\varepsilon^{4}}) complexity obtained in [ 3 ] via ULA. Our next results leverage the recent approximate RGO implementations [ 14 , 1 , 6 ] to further improve the dimension dependence. By choosing h = 1 / ( 2 ​ L ) h=1/(2L) , one can see that the RGO π X | Y = y \pi^{X\mid Y=y} is L L -strongly log-concave and 3 ​ L 3L -log-smooth, which means that it is a log-concave distribution with condition number at most 3 3 . Thus, it is natural to use existing log-concave samplers to implement the RGO. There are two main obstacles to this approach: 1. Even if we have a log-concave sampler which implements the RGO accurately in the sense of relative Fisher information, i.e., the sampler yields an approximate RGO π ^ X | Y = y \hat{\pi}^{X\mid Y=y} such that 𝖥𝖨 ( π ^ X | Y = y ∥ π X | Y = y ) ≤ δ 2 \mathsf{FI}(\hat{\pi}^{X\mid Y=y}\,\|\,\pi^{X\mid Y=y})\leq\delta^{2} , it is non-trivial to track the propagation of this error along the proximal sampler, as the relative Fisher information lacks natural properties such as a data-processing inequality. In particular, although the optimal exponent p p is still unknown, current state-of-the-art log-concave samplers achieve this high-accuracy guarantee with exponent p = 1 2 p=\frac{1}{2} [ 14 , 1 , 6 ] , which we can easily plug into the result above. Note that, up to logarithmic factors, the dependence on L / ε 2 L/\varepsilon^{2} is optimal in high dimension, in light of the lower bound of [ 11 ] . If we compare against the analogous problem of finding approximate stationary points in non-convex optimization, there the optimal complexity in high dimension is L ​ Ω 0 / ε 2 L\Omega_{0}/\varepsilon^{2} , where Ω 0 ≔ f ⁡ ( x 0 ) − inf f \Omega_{0}\coloneqq f(x_{0})-\inf f is the initial objective gap [ 5 ] . Thus, our complexity bound is entirely similar to the one in optimization, except that we incur an extra dimensional factor d p d^{p} , which is the complexity of high-accuracy log-concave sampling. Thanks to our general reduction, any improvement to the complexity of the latter task would yield an improved Fisher information complexity result for non-log-concave sampling. However, one could still ask whether there is a different approach which avoids the reduction to log-concave sampling altogether and could therefore potentially lead to improved dimension dependence. Our final result says, in essence, that the answer is no. More precisely, we show that any Fisher information complexity bound of the form ( 4 ) implies the existence of a log-concave sampler with complexity O ~ ​ ( d p ​ polylog ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) \widetilde{O}(d^{p}\polylog(1/\varepsilon)) , see Theorem 3 . This closes the loop and shows that the optimal dimension dependence for the Fisher information complexity of non-log-concave sampling, and for high-accuracy log-concave sampling, coincide.

sections.heading: 1.3 An analogy with optimization
sections.text:
There is an interesting analogy between our work on Fisher information guarantees for sampling and the study of finding approximate stationary points in optimization. As noted in Section 1.1 , it is well-established that gradient descent finds an ε \varepsilon -stationary point in O ⁡ ( 1 / ε 2 ) O(1/\varepsilon^{2}) iterations, and the lower bound of [ 5 ] shows that this is the best possible, at least in high dimension. Recent investigations, however, have focused on the complexity in low dimension, where the picture is more nuanced. To motivate this study, consider first the problem of convex, non-smooth minimization, which is a separate problem altogether but shares some similar features with the stationary point problem. In particular, gradient descent finds an ε \varepsilon -minimizer in O ⁡ ( 1 / ε 2 ) O(1/\varepsilon^{2}) steps, and lower bounds show that this is optimal in high dimension. In low dimension, however, there is a better algorithm: cutting plane methods can find an ε \varepsilon -minimizer in O ⁡ ( d ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) O(d\log(1/\varepsilon)) steps. At the level of lower bounds, this manifests in the following way: the lower bound construction in [ 5 ] showing that O ⁡ ( 1 / ε 2 ) O(1/\varepsilon^{2}) is tight is embedded in dimension d ≫ 1 / ε 2 d\gg 1/\varepsilon^{2} . The existence of the cutting plane method means that no such constructions exist when d ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ≪ 1 / ε 2 d\log(1/\varepsilon)\ll 1/\varepsilon^{2} , i.e., in dimension d ≪ 1 / ( ε 2 ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) d\ll 1/(\varepsilon^{2}\log(1/\varepsilon)) . Returning to the stationary point question, the interesting departure from the paragraph above is that thus far, we have not discovered an analogue of cutting plane methods for non-convex optimization. Indeed, the best complexities in low dimension scale as O ⁡ ( 1 / ε 2 − O ⁡ ( 1 / d ) ) O(1/\varepsilon^{2-O(1/d)}) [ 4 ] . If this is fundamental, then there should be lower bound constructions witnessing the Ω ⁡ ( 1 / ε 2 ) \Omega(1/\varepsilon^{2}) rate which can be embedded in much smaller dimension: say, d ≍ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) d\asymp\log(1/\varepsilon) or so. However, the lower bound construction of [ 5 ] requires a much larger dimension: d ≫ 1 / ε 2 d\gg 1/\varepsilon^{2} for deterministic methods, and d ≫ Ω ~ ​ ( 1 / ε 4 ) d\gg\widetilde{\Omega}(1/\varepsilon^{4}) for randomized methods. Thus, at present, it is unclear whether or not there could exist a cutting plane method for finding stationary points. More recently, [ 9 ] showed that in dimension one, when we restrict to deterministic algorithms which only use evaluations of ∇ f 
abla f (and not to evaluations of f f ), then the O ⁡ ( 1 / ε 2 ) O(1/\varepsilon^{2}) complexity is already tight; moreover, in dimension two, [ 19 ] showed that for deterministic algorithms with access to both f f and ∇ f 
abla f , the optimal complexity is Θ ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) \Theta(1/\varepsilon) . For general algorithms (randomized, with access to both f f and ∇ f 
abla f ), the optimal complexity is Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) \Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)) in dimension one [ 9 ] , Θ ⁡ ( 1 / ε 2 ) \Theta(1/\varepsilon^{2}) in large dimension ≫ Ω ~ ​ ( 1 / ε 4 ) \gg\widetilde{\Omega}(1/\varepsilon^{4}) (as discussed above), and remains open in between. As for the connection with our work: although the low-dimensional complexity of finding stationary points remains elusive in optimization, our work resolves the analogous question in the sampling setting . Indeed, the lower bound Ω ⁡ ( 1 / ε 2 − o ⁡ ( 1 ) ) \Omega(1/\varepsilon^{2-o(1)}) in [ 11 ] already holds in dimension ≫ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) / log ⁡ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) \gg\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)/\log\log(1/\varepsilon)} , and the present work shows that O ~ ​ ( 1 / ε 2 ) \widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon^{2}) can be achieved via the proximal sampler in any dimension d ≥ 1 d\geq 1 . Although this does not have direct implications for the optimization question, which remains open, we believe that this further strengthens the rich connections between the two fields.

sections.heading: 1.4 Additional related work
sections.text: First-order stationarity guarantees have also been investigated for the Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) algorithm, with initial works focusing on the kernelized Stein discrepancy (KSD), a kernelized analogue of the relative Fisher information [ 23 , 26 , 27 , 28 , 2 ] . More recently, relative Fisher information guarantees were obtained for a regularized variant of SVGD [ 17 , 16 ] . As discussed above, [ 11 ] established a lower bound on finding approximate stationary points for sampling which scales as Ω ⁡ ( ( L / ε 2 ) 1 − o ⁡ ( 1 ) ) \Omega((L/\varepsilon^{2})^{1-o(1)}) in high dimension. In addition, that paper established a second lower bound which shows that the complexity of obtaining a moderate bound of the form 𝖥𝖨 ( ⋅ ∥ π ) ≲ L d \mathsf{FI}(\cdot\,\|\,\pi)\lesssim Ld can be precisely related to the complexity of finding approximate stationary points in non-convex optimization. In particular, it implies that the Fisher information guarantee for averaged LMC in [ 3 ] is already optimal in a certain regime. However, this regime does not cover guarantees 𝖥𝖨 ( ⋅ ∥ π ) ≤ ε 2 \mathsf{FI}(\cdot\,\|\,\pi)\leq\varepsilon^{2} for small ε ≪ 1 \varepsilon\ll 1 , which is the regime of interest in this work. Moreover, their reduction is distinct from the ones we present in Theorem 2 and 3 , which relate the complexity of obtaining small Fisher information to the complexity of high-accuracy log-concave sampling.

sections.heading: 2 A review of the proximal sampler
sections.text: Throughout, we are working with standard notations and definitions, which we review in Appendix A . We review the proximal sampler algorithm, originally proposed in [ 22 ] . Our goal is to draw a sample from the target distribution π X ∝ exp ⁡ ( − f ) \pi^{X}\propto\exp(-f) supported on ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} . Let h > 0 h>0 be an arbitrary “step size”. We define the joint probability distribution π \pi on ℝ 2 ​ d \mathbb{R}^{2d} with density function: π X ​ Y ​ ( x , y ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( − f ⁡ ( x ) − 1 2 ​ h ​ ‖ x − y ‖ 2 ) . \pi^{XY}(x,y)\propto\exp\left(-f(x)-\frac{1}{2h}\|x-y\|^{2}\right). Observe that the x x -marginal of π \pi is precisely the original target distribution: π X ​ ( x ) = ∫ ℝ d π X ​ Y ​ ( x , 𝑑 y ) \pi^{X}(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\pi^{XY}(x,\mathrm{d}y) . Therefore, to sample from π X \pi^{X} , it suffices to sample ( X , Y ) ∼ π X ​ Y (X,Y)\sim\pi^{XY} and only return the X X component. To sample from π X ​ Y \pi^{XY} , [ 22 ] proposed to run Gibbs sampling with an alternating update. This results in the ideal proximal sampler algorithm, where in each iteration k ≥ 0 k\geq 0 , from the current iterate x k ∈ ℝ d x_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , we perform the following two steps: 1. Forward step: Draw y k ∣ x k ∼ π Y | X ( ⋅ ∣ x k ) = 𝒩 ( x k , h I ) y_{k}\mid x_{k}\sim\pi^{Y\mid X}(\cdot\mid x_{k})=\mathcal{N}(x_{k},hI) . 2. Backward step: Draw x k + 1 ∣ y k ∼ π X | Y ( ⋅ ∣ y k ) x_{k+1}\mid y_{k}\sim\pi^{X\mid Y}(\cdot\mid y_{k}) . By the general theory of Gibbs sampling, the Markov chain update from ( x k , y k ) (x_{k},y_{k}) to ( x k + 1 , y k + 1 ) (x_{k+1},y_{k+1}) is reversible with respect to the joint distribution π X ​ Y \pi^{XY} . We call the above the ideal proximal sampler since we assume we can implement both the forward and backward steps exactly. The forward step is easy to implement, since it only requires drawing a Gaussian distribution around the current iterate. The backward step is called the restricted Gaussian oracle (RGO) in [ 22 ] , and it is non-trivial since it requires sampling from the following probability distribution over x ∈ ℝ d x\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , for any fixed y ∈ ℝ d y\in\mathbb{R}^{d} : π X | Y ( x ∣ y ) ∝ x exp ( − f ( x ) − 1 2 ​ h ∥ x − y ∥ 2 ) . \displaystyle\pi^{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\propto_{x}\exp\left(-f(x)-\frac{1}{2h}\|x-y\|^{2}\right). (5) Note the proportionality is only over x ∈ ℝ d x\in\mathbb{R}^{d} (with fixed y ∈ ℝ d y\in\mathbb{R}^{d} ), which we denote with ∝ x \propto_{x} .

sections.text: Here, we argue that the reduction to high-accuracy log-concave sampling in Theorem 2 is the right one, by presenting a reduction in the converse direction via a simple restart strategy. We provide the proof of Theorem 3 in Appendix D.8 . Theorem 3 . Assume that there is an algorithm 𝙰𝚕𝚐 \mathtt{Alg} with the following property: for any L L -log-smooth target distribution π \pi and an initialization ρ 0 \rho_{0} satisfying 𝖪𝖫 ( ρ 0 ∥ π ) ≤ 𝖪𝖫 0 \mathsf{KL}(\rho_{0}\,\|\,\pi)\leq\mathsf{KL}_{0} , ℛ 2 ( ρ 0 ∥ π ) ≤ Δ 0 \mathcal{R}_{2}(\rho_{0}\,\|\,\pi)\leq\Delta_{0} , 𝙰𝚕𝚐 \mathtt{Alg} outputs a sample from a distribution π ^ \widehat{\pi} with ℛ 2 ( π ^ ∥ π ) ≤ Δ 0 \mathcal{R}_{2}(\widehat{\pi}\,\|\,\pi)\leq\Delta_{0} and 𝖥𝖨 ( π ^ ∥ π ) ≤ ε 2 \mathsf{FI}(\widehat{\pi}\,\|\,\pi)\leq\varepsilon^{2} using L ​ 𝖪𝖫 0 ε 2 ​ ϕ ​ ( d ) ​ polylog ⁡ ( Δ 0 , L / ε 2 ) \frac{L\,\mathsf{KL}_{0}}{\varepsilon^{2}}\,\phi(d)\polylog(\Delta_{0},L/\varepsilon^{2}) queries to an oracle for π \pi . Then, there is another algorithm 𝙰𝚕𝚐 ′ \mathtt{Alg}^{\prime} with the following property: for any α \alpha -strongly log-concave and L L -log-smooth distribution π \pi with mode at the origin, 𝙰𝚕𝚐 ′ \mathtt{Alg}^{\prime} outputs a sample from a distribution π ^ \widehat{\pi} with 𝖪𝖫 ( π ^ ∥ π ) ≤ ε 2 \mathsf{KL}(\widehat{\pi}\,\|\,\pi)\leq\varepsilon^{2} using O ⁡ ( κ ​ ϕ ​ ( d ) ​ polylog ⁡ ( d , κ , 1 ε ) ) O(\kappa\,\phi(d)\polylog(d,\kappa,\frac{1}{\varepsilon})) queries to the same oracle for π \pi , where κ ≔ L α \kappa\coloneqq\frac{L}{\alpha} is the condition number. Note that, aside from the technical condition that 𝙰𝚕𝚐 \mathtt{Alg} satisfies ℛ 2 ( π ^ ∥ π ) ≤ Δ 0 \mathcal{R}_{2}(\widehat{\pi}\,\|\,\pi)\leq\Delta_{0} , the conclusion of Theorem 2 satisfies the requirement of 𝙰𝚕𝚐 \mathtt{Alg} with ϕ ​ ( d ) = O ~ ​ ( d ) \phi(d)=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d}) , which by Theorem 3 leads to a high-accuracy log-concave sampler with complexity O ~ ​ ( κ ​ d ) \widetilde{O}(\kappa\sqrt{d}) . Morally, the conclusion is that the dimension dependence in Theorem 2 cannot be improved without also improving the dimension dependence of high-accuracy log-concave sampling. However, we note that there is a slight gap: Theorem 2 assumes the existence of a ℛ 3 \mathcal{R}_{3} sampler, whereas the output of Theorem 3 is only a 𝖪𝖫 \mathsf{KL} sampler. We do not view this issue as fundamental, as there seems to not be any reason to expect the complexity of sampling in 𝖪𝖫 \mathsf{KL} vs. ℛ q \mathcal{R}_{q} to be substantially different: indeed, guarantees which are initially proven in 𝖪𝖫 \mathsf{KL} are often later improved to hold in ℛ q \mathcal{R}_{q} . Moreover, a 𝖪𝖫 \mathsf{KL} guarantee can usually be boosted to a ℛ 3 \mathcal{R}_{3} guarantee, provided that we have a warm start in a slightly stronger Rényi divergence such as ℛ 4 \mathcal{R}_{4} ; see the argument of [ 1 , Lemma 5.2] . Therefore, Theorem 3 should also imply the existence of a ℛ 3 \mathcal{R}_{3} sampler with complexity O ~ ​ ( κ ​ ϕ ​ ( d ) ) \widetilde{O}(\kappa\phi(d)) from a suitable warm start.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we obtained a new complexity bound for sampling from a measure with small relative Fisher information to the target, which can be interpreted as an approximate first-order stationary measure for sampling. Our bound, which is based on the proximal sampler, is near-optimal in its dependence on the precision ε \varepsilon . Moreover, the dimension dependence of our bound matches the dimension dependence of high-accuracy log-concave sampling, and the former cannot be improved without also improving the latter. This provides a relatively complete picture of the Fisher information complexity of sampling. Going forward, one interesting open problem is to improve the Fisher information lower bound of [ 11 ] to exhibit polynomial dependence on the dimension since, by our results, it would imply a corresponding lower bound with polynomial dimension dependence for high-accuracy log-concave sampling. Another open problem is to determine the optimal Fisher information complexity in dimension one (see [ 11 ] ).

August 24, 2026 Abstract We study the query complexity of obtaining a relative Fisher information guarantee for sampling from a log-smooth non-log-concave distribution; this is a sampling analog of finding an approximate stationary point in optimization. Our algorithm is based on the proximal sampler, which is an implicit discretization of the Langevin diffusion, and requires an implementation of the backward step known as the restricted Gaussian oracle (RGO). We show that by leveraging the recent results for log-concave sampling with high-accuracy guarantees in Rényi divergence, we can obtain an approximate RGO implementation that—when used with the proximal sampler—yields a complexity guarantee in relative Fisher information that inherits the same dimension dependence as log-concave sampling, and improves upon prior work for non-log-concave sampling. We also show a converse reduction that any improvement in the dimension dependence in relative Fisher information for non-log-concave sampling will yield an improved dimension dependence for high-accuracy log-concave sampling. 1 Introduction 1.1 Motivation and background What is the complexity of sampling from a smooth distribution π ∝ exp ⁡ ( − f ) \pi\propto\exp(-f) over ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} ? When π \pi is log-concave or satisfies an isoperimetric inequality, then this question is well-studied, with many results providing iteration complexity guarantees which scale polynomially in the dimension and the isoperimetric constants; see [ 13 ] for an introduction to some of these developments. In this case, simple worst-case examples demonstrate that generating a sample close in total variation distance to π \pi can require exponentially many queries to f f (e.g., with respect to the ambient dimension d d ; see [ 18 ] .). One way to overcome this difficulty is to impose additional problem structure, such as assuming that π \pi is a mixture of strongly log-concave distributions [ 21 ] or to assume that an annealing path has small “action” [ 15 ] , which requires designing tailor-made algorithms for each problem class under consideration. Another approach is to weaken the notion of progress by seeking an approximately “stationary” solution. The latter idea has been especially fruitful in the sister field of optimization [ 24 ] , namely to minimize (or find a stationary point of) an objective function f : ℝ d → ℝ f\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}	o\mathbb{R} , in which the corresponding question becomes: How many queries to ∇ f

In the case where f f is L L -smooth but potentially non-convex, gradient descent finds such an approximate stationary point in O ⁡ ( 1 / ε 2 ) O(1/\varepsilon^{2}) iterations, and this rate is optimal in high dimension [ 5 ] . The optimal complexity in low dimension is still open, and it turns out that the results of this paper take on an interesting interpretation in light of this story; see Section 1.3 below. Although finding a stationary point is still a far cry from finding a global optimum, it is often the starting point for deeper investigations, such as the development of algorithms which escape “undesirable” stationary points (e.g., strict saddles). More broadly, this theory has the advantage of having great generality, as it is one of the few frameworks available to quantitatively study general non-convex optimization problems. Developing an analogous theory for the task of sampling is more subtle, as one must first decide on a suitable definition of an “approximate stationary point”. As noted in Section 1.1 , it is well-established that gradient descent finds an ε \varepsilon -stationary point in O ⁡ ( 1 / ε 2 ) O(1/\varepsilon^{2}) iterations, and the lower bound of [ 5 ] shows that this is the best possible, at least in high dimension. Recent investigations, however, have focused on the complexity in low dimension, where the picture is more nuanced. To motivate this study, consider first the problem of convex, non-smooth minimization, which is a separate problem altogether but shares some similar features with the stationary point problem. In particular, gradient descent finds an ε \varepsilon -minimizer in O ⁡ ( 1 / ε 2 ) O(1/\varepsilon^{2}) steps, and lower bounds show that this is optimal in high dimension.
